title: PHY_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: Which statement expresses the quantisation of electric charge?
options: Charges combine by the algebraic addition of their signed magnitudes.
The total charge of an isolated system does not change with time.
Charge exists only as a whole-number multiple of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Charge is a scalar quantity and so has magnitude but no direction.
questions.why: Why C is right: quantisation means charge comes only in whole multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so Q = ne with n an integer. Why the others are wrong: A is additivity, the rule that charges add algebraically with sign · B is conservation, that total charge in an isolated system is fixed · D is true of charge but is the scalar property, not quantisation.

questions.q: A rod carrying a negative charge is touched briefly to a neutral insulated metal sphere and then taken away. The sphere is left
options: negatively charged, the same sign as the rod.
positively charged, the opposite sign to the rod.
neutral overall, with negative charge gathered on the near side.
neutral, because charge cannot cross a point of contact.
questions.why: Why A is right: contact is charging by conduction. Charge flows across and is shared, so both objects end with the same sign as the original rod — negative. Why the others are wrong: B is the result of charging by *induction*, the classic conduction/induction reversal · C describes polarisation, which happens when the rod is brought near but not touched · D denies that charge crosses a conducting contact, which it plainly does.

questions.q: A body carries a net charge of −4.8 μC. How many excess electrons does it hold?
questions.why: Why D is right: n = |Q|/e = (4.8 × 10⁻⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹). 4.8/1.6 = 3.0 and 10⁻⁶/10⁻¹⁹ = 10¹³, so n = 3.0 × 10¹³ electrons, a pure count with no units. Why the others are wrong: A treats μC as nC, losing three powers of ten · B multiplies by e instead of dividing (4.8 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 7.7 × 10⁻²⁵) · C inverts the mantissa division, using 1.6/4.8 = 0.33 rather than 4.8/1.6.

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is held near an insulated metal sphere, which is then connected to earth. To leave the sphere positively charged, the correct sequence is to
options: withdraw the rod, then disconnect the earth wire.
disconnect the earth wire while the rod is still near, then withdraw the rod.
disconnect the earth wire and withdraw the rod at the same instant.
connect the earth wire only after the rod has been withdrawn.
questions.why: Why B is right: with the negative rod still near, the repelled electrons have escaped to earth. Breaking the earth connection first traps the deficit, and only then may the rod be withdrawn, leaving a net positive sphere. Why the others are wrong: A withdraws the rod first, so the electrons flow straight back up the earth wire and the sphere ends neutral · C is the same failure, since removing them together gives the electrons a return path at the moment the rod's influence goes · D earths a sphere with no rod near it, which does nothing at all.

questions.q: A body that acquires a positive charge by friction has
options: gained protons transferred from the other body.
lost some of its electrons to the other body.
lost some of its protons to the other body.
had some of its neutrons converted into protons.
questions.why: Why B is right: protons are locked in the nucleus; only electrons move. Positive means a deficit of electrons. Why the others are wrong: A and C both move protons between bodies, which never happens in friction · D invents a nuclear reaction to explain an electrostatic effect.

questions.q: Two identical metal spheres carry +8.0 μC and −2.0 μC. They are brought into contact and then separated. Each sphere now carries
options: +3.0 μC on one and −3.0 μC on the other.
questions.why: Why D is right: charge is conserved, so the total is (+8.0) + (−2.0) = +6.0 μC. The spheres are identical, so they share equally: +3.0 μC each. Why the others are wrong: A finds the correct total but forgets to halve it · B averages the two *magnitudes*, (8 + 2)/2, ignoring the minus sign · C keeps the charges equal and opposite, treating contact as a swap rather than a sharing. ### Week 2 — Coulomb's law, superposition and the electric field

questions.q: Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is
options: proportional to the product of their magnitudes, inversely proportional to the square of their separation, and directed along the line joining them.
proportional to the sum of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to their separation.
proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to their separation, along the line of centres.
proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, directed at right angles to the line of centres.
questions.why: Why A is right: the law needs all three parts — proportional to the product of the magnitudes, inversely proportional to the *square* of the separation, and directed along the line of centres. Why the others are wrong: B uses the sum of the charges and drops the square · C drops the square, the single commonest omission in the course · D has the physics right but the direction wrong; the force acts along the line joining the charges, never across it.

questions.q: The permittivity of free space ε₀ has the value
options: 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²
4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A
questions.why: Why C is right: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²), and k = 1/(4πε₀). Why the others are wrong: A is k itself, the standard ε₀/k swap, which scales any answer by 4π · B is μ₀, the magnetic constant · D is Planck's constant.

questions.q: Point charges of +3.0 μC and −5.0 μC are 0.20 m apart in vacuum. The force between them is
options: 3.37 N, repulsive
3.37 N, attractive
0.674 N, attractive
0.135 N, attractive
questions.why: Why B is right: F = kq₁q₂/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = 0.1349/0.0400 = 3.37 N. The charges are unlike, so the force is attractive. Why the others are wrong: A has the right size but calls unlike charges repulsive · C divides by r instead of r², giving 0.674 N · D never divides by the separation at all, leaving the numerator 0.135 N.

questions.q: A point charge of 4.0 nC sits in vacuum. The magnitude of the electric field 3.0 cm from it is
questions.why: Why A is right: E = kQ/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.030)² = 35.96/9.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Why the others are wrong: B forgets to square r (35.96/0.030) · C divides by ε₀ instead of multiplying by k, inflating the answer by the factor 4π ≈ 12.6 · D leaves r in centimetres, dividing by 9 rather than 9.0 × 10⁻⁴.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the electric field E from the electric force F?
options: E acts only on positive charges, while F acts on charges of either sign.
E is measured in newtons, while F is measured in newtons per coulomb.
E is a scalar quantity, while F is a vector with magnitude and direction.
E exists at a point with or without a charge there; F needs a charge.
questions.why: Why D is right: the field is a property of the space around a charge and exists whether or not a test charge is placed in it; the force appears only once a charge is actually there. Why the others are wrong: A invents a sign restriction; E exerts force on charges of either sign · B reverses the units — E is N/C and F is N · C reverses the vector status; both E and F are vectors.

questions.q: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
options: They may cross where the fields of two charges are equal in magnitude.
They begin on negative charge and terminate on positive charge.
Their direction at a point is that of the force on a positive test charge.
They are drawn closer together in regions where the field is weaker.
questions.why: Why C is right: by definition a field line's direction is the direction of the force on a *positive* test charge placed there. Why the others are wrong: A allows lines to cross, which would give the field two directions at one point · B reverses the convention; lines start on positive and end on negative · D reverses the density rule; closer lines mean a *stronger* field.

questions.q: A charge of +4.0 nC is at x = 0 and a charge of +9.0 nC is at x = 0.50 m. On the line between them the resultant field is zero at
questions.why: Why A is right: between two like charges the fields oppose, so set kQ₁/x² = kQ₂/(0.50 − x)². Then 4/x² = 9/(0.50 − x)², so 2/x = 3/(0.50 − x), giving 1.00 − 2x = 3x and x = 0.20 m from the 4.0 nC charge. Why the others are wrong: B is 0.30 m, the mirror-image answer you get by placing the null point nearer the *larger* charge · C is the midpoint, which would only be the answer for equal charges · D looks outside the pair, which is where the null point sits for *unlike* charges, not like ones.

questions.q: An electron is released in a uniform electric field that points due east. The electron
options: accelerates due east, along the direction of the field.
accelerates due west, against the direction of the field.
moves in a circle, because the force is perpendicular to the field.
stays at rest, because a field acts only on positive charges.
questions.why: Why B is right: the electron is negative, so F = qE points opposite to E — westwards. Why the others are wrong: A forgets the sign of the electron and follows the field · C imports the circular motion of a magnetic field, where the force is perpendicular to the velocity · D wrongly claims a field acts only on positive charge.

questions.q: The principle of superposition states that the resultant electric field at a point due to several charges is
options: the algebraic sum of the magnitudes of the individual fields.
the field of the nearest charge, the others being screened by it.
the vector sum of the fields each charge would produce alone.
the average of the fields the individual charges would produce.
questions.why: Why C is right: superposition says each pair acts independently and the contributions are added *as vectors*, with directions, not as bare numbers. Why the others are wrong: A adds magnitudes, which gives the wrong answer whenever contributions partly oppose · B invents electrostatic screening between free charges · D averages instead of summing. ### Week 3 — Electromotive force, internal resistance, conductors and insulators

questions.q: The electromotive force of a source is best defined as
options: the energy supplied by the source per unit charge passing through it.
the force with which the source drives charge round the circuit, in newtons.
the potential difference across its terminals while it delivers current.
the total chemical energy stored inside the source, measured in joules.
questions.why: Why A is right: emf is the energy the source gives each coulomb passing through it — joules per coulomb, which is the volt. Why the others are wrong: B treats emf as a literal force and quotes newtons, the trap the name sets · C defines terminal potential difference, which equals ε only at zero current · D gives total stored energy in joules, not energy per unit charge.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of electromotive force is
options: M¹ L² T⁻²
M¹ L¹ T⁻² I⁻¹
M¹ L² T⁻² I⁻¹
M¹ L² T⁻³ I⁻¹
questions.why: Why D is right: work has dimensions M¹L²T⁻², charge is I¹T¹, so emf = work/charge = M¹L²T⁻³I⁻¹ — the same as potential difference, as it must be. Why the others are wrong: A is the dimension of work or energy, forgetting to divide by charge · B divides by length rather than squaring it · C divides by current but not by time, the commonest slip in the derivation.

questions.q: A cell of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to an 8.0 Ω resistor. The terminal potential difference is
questions.why: Why B is right: I = ε/(R + r) = 9.0/(8.0 + 1.0) = 1.00 A, so V = ε − Ir = 9.0 − (1.00)(1.0) = 8.0 V. Cross-check: IR = (1.00)(8.0) = 8.0 V. Why the others are wrong: A ignores the internal resistance entirely, giving V = ε · C uses R alone to find the current (9.0/8.0 = 1.125 A) and then subtracts, giving 7.88 V · D writes V = ε + Ir, so the internal drop is added instead of subtracted — a loaded cell can never read above its emf.

questions.q: For a cell under varying load, terminal voltage V is plotted against current I. The straight line obtained has
options: a gradient equal to the emf and an intercept equal to the internal resistance.
a gradient of +r and an intercept on the V-axis equal to the emf.
an intercept on the V-axis equal to ε and a gradient of −r.
an intercept on the I-axis equal to ε and a gradient of −R.
questions.why: Why C is right: V = ε − Ir is a straight line in I. At I = 0 the reading is ε, so the V-intercept is the emf; the coefficient of I is −r, so the gradient is minus the internal resistance. Why the others are wrong: A swaps intercept and gradient · B gets the sign of the gradient wrong; the line slopes *down* as the load current rises · D reads ε off the wrong axis and confuses r with the external R.

questions.q: A straight rod 0.25 m long moves at 6.0 m/s perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.40 T. The emf generated between its ends is
questions.why: Why D is right: ε = Bvl = (0.40)(6.0)(0.25) = 0.60 V. Why the others are wrong: A drops the length, computing Bv = 2.4 · B drops the flux density, computing vl = 1.5 · C is a straight power-of-ten slip on the correct value.

questions.q: An electromagnetic flow meter measures liquid flow by detecting the emf ε = Bvl generated across the pipe. It fails on distilled water because distilled water
options: has too low a density to generate a measurable emf.
carries almost no free ions, so no charge is swept to the electrodes.
is not magnetic, so the field cannot penetrate it.
flows too smoothly for the magnetic field through it to change.
questions.why: Why B is right: the meter works because the *liquid itself* is the moving conductor; charge must be swept to the electrodes. Distilled water carries almost no ions, so nothing is swept and no emf appears. The same failure applies to hydrocarbons. Why the others are wrong: A blames density, which does not enter ε = Bvl at all · C confuses electrical conduction with ferromagnetism; the field passes through water perfectly well · D invents a turbulence requirement, but this meter needs no change of field, only motion of charge.

questions.q: Why is the electric field zero inside a metal in electrostatic equilibrium?
options: A metal contains no charges capable of setting up an electric field at all.
The nuclei and the free electrons are equal in number at every point in the metal.
The resistivity of a metal is so low that no potential difference can exist across it.
Any interior field would move the free electrons until they cancelled it.
questions.why: Why D is right: this is the self-correcting argument. Any interior field would push the free electrons, and they would keep moving until their redistribution cancelled it. In the steady state, therefore, the field must already be zero. Why the others are wrong: A is false; a metal is full of mobile charge · B is a static claim that does not explain why the redistribution happens · C confuses low resistivity with zero field and ignores that a current-carrying conductor *does* have a field inside it.

questions.q: Excess charge given to a solid metal sphere in electrostatic equilibrium settles
options: uniformly throughout the whole volume of the sphere.
at the centre, as far as possible from the surroundings.
entirely on the outer surface.
in a thin shell just below the surface, leaving the surface itself neutral.
questions.why: Why C is right: charge inside the bulk would set up a field there, which cannot exist in equilibrium, so all excess charge migrates to the outer surface. Why the others are wrong: A spreads it through the volume, which would give a non-zero internal field · B puts it at the centre, the worst case for mutual repulsion · D invents a sub-surface shell; the charge sits on the surface itself.

questions.q: When the temperature is raised, the resistance of
options: a metal rises, while that of a semiconductor falls.
a metal falls, while that of a semiconductor rises.
both a metal and a semiconductor rises.
both a metal and a semiconductor falls.
questions.why: Why A is right: in a metal, heating makes the lattice vibrate more and scatter the drifting electrons, so R rises. In a semiconductor, heating frees more carriers, so R falls. Why the others are wrong: B reverses both, the single most common error on this point · C and D make the two materials behave alike, which is exactly what the question tests against. ### Week 4 — Capacitance, dielectrics and the electric dipole

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 0.0050 m. Its capacitance is
questions.why: Why A is right: C = ε₀A/d = (8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(0.020)/(0.0050) = 1.77 × 10⁻¹³/5.0 × 10⁻³ = 3.54 × 10⁻¹¹ F, that is 35.4 pF. Why the others are wrong: B is the value the course slides give, wrong by exactly one power of ten — checking U two ways exposes it · C inverts A and d, computing ε₀d/A = 2.21 × 10⁻¹² F · D is a further power-of-ten slip in the opposite direction.

questions.q: The capacitance of a capacitor is defined as
options: the largest charge it can hold before its dielectric breaks down.
the energy it stores when the potential difference across it is one volt.
the charge on either plate per unit potential difference between the plates.
the net charge on the capacitor divided by the field between its plates.
questions.why: Why C is right: capacitance is charge stored per unit potential difference, C = Q/V, where Q is the charge on *either* plate. Why the others are wrong: A describes the breakdown limit, a different property · B describes stored energy, which goes as V², not as V · D divides charge by field rather than by potential difference, and also says "net charge", which for a capacitor is zero.

questions.q: Two capacitors joined in series have a combined capacitance that is
options: the sum of the two, and always larger than either of them.
smaller than either of them, found from 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
the product divided by the sum, and always larger than either of them.
equal to the larger of the two capacitances.
questions.why: Why B is right: capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors. In series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂, so the total is always *smaller* than the smaller of the two. Why the others are wrong: A applies the resistor series rule, the most-examined trap on this topic · C uses the product-over-sum formula, which is correct for series capacitors in value but the stated conclusion "larger than either" is false — it is always smaller · D simply picks the larger capacitor.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged and then disconnected from the battery. Its plates are then pulled further apart. The energy stored
options: falls, because the capacitance falls and U = ½CV².
is unchanged, because the charge on the plates is unchanged.
falls, because the field between the plates weakens with distance.
rises, because Q is fixed while C falls, and U = Q²/2C.
questions.why: Why D is right: disconnected means Q is fixed. Pulling the plates apart raises d, so C = ε₀A/d falls, and with Q fixed the right form is U = Q²/2C, which rises. Physically, you do work pulling apart plates that attract. Why the others are wrong: A uses ½CV² while treating V as constant, but V is not constant once the battery is removed · B confuses constant charge with constant energy · C assumes the field weakens with separation, but for parallel plates at fixed Q the field is unchanged; it is V = Ed that grows.

questions.q: A dielectric slab is slid between the plates of a charged, disconnected capacitor. The capacitance rises because the slab
options: polarises, so bound charge weakens the net field and lowers V.
supplies extra free electrons which add to the charge already on the plates.
conducts a little, letting charge move directly between the two plates.
strengthens the field between the plates and so raises the charge stored.
questions.why: Why A is right: the dielectric has no free electrons, but its bound charges shift, and that polarisation sets up an opposing field. The net field falls, so V falls, and since C = Q/V with Q fixed, C rises. Why the others are wrong: B has the dielectric donating free charge, which an insulator by definition cannot do · C makes the dielectric a conductor, which would discharge the capacitor rather than improve it · D reverses the field effect; a dielectric *reduces* the field between the plates.

questions.q: The electric field in a region of vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁵ V/m. The energy stored per unit volume is
questions.why: Why B is right: u = ½ε₀E² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(3.0 × 10⁵)² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(9.0 × 10¹⁰) = 0.398 J/m³. Why the others are wrong: A drops the factor of ½ · C fails to square E, giving 1.33 × 10⁻⁶ · D is the right number with the wrong unit — the slides make exactly this mistake, calling the density a total energy; the total is u × Ad.

questions.q: The electric dipole moment of a pair of charges +q and −q separated by a distance d is
options: 2qd, directed from the positive charge to the negative charge, in C·m.
qd, directed from the positive charge to the negative charge, in C/m.
qd, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge, in C·m.
2qd, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge, in N·m.
questions.why: Why C is right: p = qd, using the magnitude of *one* charge times the separation, in coulomb-metres, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge in the physics convention. Why the others are wrong: A uses 2q, doubling the moment, and reverses the direction to the chemistry convention · B has the right magnitude but the reversed direction and the wrong unit, C/m instead of C·m · D combines the doubled charge with a torque unit, N·m.

questions.q: A dipole of charges ±3.0 nC separated by 2.0 mm lies in a uniform field of 4.0 × 10⁵ N/C with its axis at 30° to the field. The torque on it is
questions.why: Why A is right: p = qd = (3.0 × 10⁻⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 6.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, and τ = pE sin θ = (6.0 × 10⁻¹²)(4.0 × 10⁵)(sin 30°) = (2.4 × 10⁻⁶)(0.500) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ N·m. Why the others are wrong: B omits sin θ, which would only be right at 90° · C uses cos 30° = 0.866 instead of sin 30°, measuring θ from the wrong line · D leaves the separation in millimetres, inflating p by 10³.

questions.q: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field with its axis at 90° to the field. It experiences
options: a net force along the field and no torque.
neither a net force nor a torque.
a net force along the field together with a torque.
a torque but no net force.
questions.why: Why D is right: in a *uniform* field the two forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero; but they act at different points, forming a couple, so a torque remains — at 90° it is at its maximum, pE. Why the others are wrong: A and C give a net force, which requires a *non-uniform* field · B claims no torque, which is only true when p is already aligned with E.

questions.q: At a point on the perpendicular bisector of a short dipole,
options: both V and E are zero.
V is zero but E is not, and E points opposite to p.
E is zero but V is not, and V there is negative.
both V and E take their maximum values for that distance.
questions.why: Why B is right: on the perpendicular bisector each point is equally far from +q and −q, so +kq/r and −kq/r cancel exactly and V = 0. The fields do not cancel: their axial components add, giving a resultant pointing opposite to p. Why the others are wrong: A makes the standard inference that V = 0 implies E = 0, which is exactly what this geometry disproves · C swaps the two quantities · D says V is maximum, when it is precisely zero there. ### Week 5 — DC circuits: series, parallel and Kirchhoff's rules

questions.q: The power dissipated in a resistor R across which there is a potential difference V is
options: V/R
VR²
V²R
V²/R
questions.why: Why D is right: from P = VI and V = IR, substituting I = V/R gives P = V²/R. Why the others are wrong: A is the current, not the power · B and C put R in the wrong place — B multiplies by R² and C by R, both of which fail dimensionally; power must fall as R rises at fixed V.

questions.q: In a circuit, resistors connected in series all have the same
options: potential difference across them, while resistors in parallel all carry the same current.
current through them, while resistors in parallel all have the same potential difference.
power dissipated in them, while resistors in parallel all have the same resistance.
resistance as one another, while resistors in parallel all carry the same current.
questions.why: Why B is right: a series chain offers one path, so the current is common and the voltages add; parallel branches share the same two nodes, so the voltage is common and the currents add. Why the others are wrong: A swaps the two, the most frequent confusion in circuit work · C claims equal power in series, which is false unless the resistances are equal · D asserts the resistances themselves must be equal, which is not required in either arrangement.

questions.q: Resistors of 12 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 4.0 Ω are connected in parallel. Their combined resistance is
questions.why: Why C is right: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/6 + 1/4 = (1 + 2 + 3)/12 = 6/12, so R = 2.0 Ω — smaller than the smallest resistor, as a parallel total always must be. Why the others are wrong: A adds them as if in series · B computes 1/R = 0.50 Ω⁻¹ and forgets to invert · D takes the mean, 22/3.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a statement of the conservation of
options: charge, since charge cannot accumulate at a point.
energy, since a charge returns to its starting potential.
momentum, since the drifting electrons collide elastically.
power, since the power entering equals the power leaving.
questions.why: Why A is right: the junction rule ΣI_in = ΣI_out says charge cannot pile up at a point, which is conservation of charge. Why the others are wrong: B is the conservation law behind the *loop* rule, not the junction rule · C invents a mechanical law that plays no part here · D is not a conservation law of the circuit; power in a junction is not conserved branch by branch in this sense.

questions.q: Travelling round a loop in the same direction as the assumed current, the potential change across a resistor R carrying current I is written as
options: +IR, because the current is doing work there.
+I²R, because the resistor dissipates power.
zero, because the loop rule already allows for it.
−IR, because potential falls along the current.
questions.why: Why D is right: current flows from high to low potential through a resistor, so travelling *with* the current means going downhill: the change is −IR. Why the others are wrong: A has the sign reversed, which is the rule for travelling *against* the assumed current · B substitutes a power, not a potential change, and gets the units wrong · C claims the resistor contributes nothing, which would leave nothing to balance the emf.

questions.q: Solving a Kirchhoff network gives one branch current as −0.67 A. This means that
options: the working contains a sign error and must be repeated from the start.
the branch carries no current, and 0.67 A is dissipated as heat instead.
the branch carries 0.67 A opposite to the assumed direction.
the emf in that branch has been connected the wrong way round.
questions.why: Why C is right: the assumed direction is a guess. A negative result is a correct answer meaning "that magnitude, the other way round" — here 0.67 A flowing against the arrow you drew. Why the others are wrong: A treats a legitimate result as an error and invites the student to "fix" the signs, which corrupts the solution · B invents a heat mechanism to dispose of the current · D blames the battery's polarity, which was given in the question and is not what the minus sign reports.

questions.q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance drives a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. The current in the 6.0 Ω resistor is
questions.why: Why A is right: 6.0 ∥ 3.0 = (6 × 3)/9 = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω and the supply current is 12/6.0 = 2.0 A. The voltage across the parallel section is (2.0)(2.0) = 4.0 V, so the current in the 6.0 Ω branch is 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A. Why the others are wrong: B is the total supply current, taken as if all of it went through the 6.0 Ω · C is the current in the 3.0 Ω branch, the two swapped · D comes from using 12 V across the parallel section instead of the 4.0 V that actually appears there.

questions.q: In applying the superposition theorem to a linear circuit, an ideal voltage source that is not being considered is replaced by
options: an open circuit.
a resistor equal in value to the load resistance.
a short circuit.
an ideal current source of the same magnitude.
questions.why: Why C is right: zeroing an ideal voltage source means forcing zero volts between its terminals, which is exactly what a wire does — a short circuit. Why the others are wrong: A is the correct treatment for a zeroed *current* source, the classic reversal · B leaves a resistance behind that was never there · D substitutes one active source for another, which does not zero anything. ### Week 6 — Alternating current: peak and rms values

questions.q: The rms value of an alternating current is
options: the average of all instantaneous values taken over one complete cycle.
the steady direct current dissipating the same average power in the same resistor.
the peak value divided by two, since only half the cycle is positive.
the largest instantaneous value the current reaches in a cycle.
questions.why: Why B is right: rms is defined through power — it is the steady DC that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistor. Why the others are wrong: A gives the plain mean, which for a full sine cycle is zero · C invents a factor of two; the factor is √2, and it comes from the mean of the *square* · D defines the peak value, not the rms value.

questions.q: The Nigerian mains supply is quoted as 230 V. The peak voltage the insulation must withstand is
questions.why: Why D is right: a quoted supply voltage is rms, so V_max = √2 × V_rms = 1.414 × 230 = 325 V. Why the others are wrong: A divides by √2 instead of multiplying, giving 163 V — but the peak must always exceed the rms · B assumes the quoted figure is already the peak · C doubles instead of applying √2.

questions.q: The mean value of a sinusoidal current over a full cycle is zero, yet the current heats a resistor throughout. This is because
options: the resistor stores energy in the negative half-cycle and releases it in the positive half.
power depends on i², and the square of a negative current is positive.
only the positive half of each cycle actually passes through the resistor.
the resistance of the resistor becomes negative during the negative half-cycle.
questions.why: Why B is right: heating depends on i²R, and squaring makes every instantaneous value positive, so the negative half-cycle heats exactly as much as the positive one. Why the others are wrong: A treats a resistor as an energy store, which is what a reactance does, not a resistor · C claims half the cycle does not flow, but current flows throughout, merely reversing · D invents a negative resistance.

questions.q: In a purely resistive AC circuit the average power is exactly half the maximum instantaneous power, because
options: both V and I are smaller than their peak values by a factor of √2.
the current flows for only half of each complete cycle.
the power is negative for half the cycle and positive for the other half.
the resistor returns half the energy it receives back to the supply.
questions.why: Why A is right: P_avg = V_rms I_rms = (V_max/√2)(I_max/√2) = V_max I_max/2, exactly half the peak power. The two factors of √2 are the whole reason. Why the others are wrong: B halves the *time*, but current flows in both halves of the cycle · C describes a reactive circuit, where power really does go negative; in a pure resistor it never does · D has the resistor returning energy, which only a capacitor or inductor does.

questions.q: In the expression v = V_max sin ωt, the quantity ω is
options: the frequency in hertz, equal to 1/T.
the phase angle between the voltage and the current.
the period of the waveform, measured in seconds.
the angular frequency, equal to 2πf, in rad/s.
questions.why: Why D is right: ω is the angular frequency, ω = 2πf = 2π/T, measured in radians per second. Why the others are wrong: A confuses ω with f, an error of 2π wherever it is substituted · B confuses it with the phase angle φ · C confuses it with the period, whose units are seconds, not rad/s.

questions.q: As the frequency of the supply is raised,
options: both X_L and X_C increase.
X_L decreases and X_C increases.
X_L increases and X_C decreases.
both remain unchanged, since both are measured in ohms.
questions.why: Why C is right: X_L = ωL rises with frequency, because a coil fights faster changes of current harder; X_C = 1/(ωC) falls with frequency, because the plates have less time to charge. Why the others are wrong: A and B each get one of the two backwards, B reversing both · D confuses having the same unit as resistance with behaving like resistance; only R is frequency-independent.

questions.q: In a purely capacitive AC circuit,
options: the current leads the voltage by 90°.
the voltage leads the current by 90°.
the current and the voltage are in phase.
the current lags the voltage by 180°.
questions.why: Why A is right: charge must arrive before a voltage can build across the plates, so the current comes first — in a capacitor, I leads V, the C-I-V of the CIVIL mnemonic. Why the others are wrong: B is the inductor's behaviour, the classic lead/lag reversal · C describes a pure resistor · D uses 180°, but a pure reactance shifts the phase by a quarter cycle, 90°, not a half.

questions.q: A 20.0 μF capacitor is connected to a 50.0 Hz supply. Its reactance is
questions.why: Why B is right: ω = 2π(50.0) = 314.2 rad/s, ωC = (314.2)(20.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 6.283 × 10⁻³, so X_C = 1/(6.283 × 10⁻³) = 159 Ω. Why the others are wrong: A is ωC itself — the reciprocal was never taken · C uses f in place of ω, giving 1/(fC) = 1000 Ω, an error of 2π · D is a mangled halving of A and is likewise a reactance never inverted. ### Week 7 — Power in AC circuits, reactance and resonance

questions.q: The power factor of an AC circuit is
options: the ratio of the apparent power to the real power.
the ratio of the peak power to the average power.
the sine of the phase angle between voltage and current.
the ratio of real power to apparent power, equal to cos φ.
questions.why: Why D is right: the power factor is PF = P/S = cos φ, real power divided by apparent power. It is 1 for a pure resistor and 0 for a pure reactance. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the ratio, which would give values above 1 · B compares peak with average power, a different ratio that is 2 in a resistive circuit · C uses sin φ, which belongs to the *reactive* power, not the power factor.

questions.q: The average real power consumed by an ideal capacitor in an AC circuit is
options: V_rms I_rms sin φ, which is the reactive power.
zero, because energy is stored and returned each quarter-cycle.
V_rms I_rms, since neither the current nor the voltage is zero.
half of V_rms I_rms, averaged across the whole cycle.
questions.why: Why B is right: an ideal capacitor's current is 90° out of phase with its voltage, so cos φ = 0 and the average real power is zero. Energy flows in during one quarter-cycle and straight back out the next. Why the others are wrong: A is the reactive power in VAR, which the Week 7 slides wrongly label as real power; real power always uses cos φ · C is the apparent power, which is non-zero but is not what is consumed · D halves the apparent power for no reason.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 50.0 Ω, X_L = 31.4 Ω and X_C = 159 Ω. Its impedance is
questions.why: Why C is right: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) = √(50.0² + (31.4 − 159)²) = √(2500 + 16 282) = √18 782 = 137 Ω. The sign of the reactance difference disappears in the squaring. Why the others are wrong: A adds R, X_L and X_C arithmetically, which ignores the 90° phase differences · B subtracts them arithmetically, |50.0 + 31.4 − 159| = 77.6 Ω · D adds the reactances instead of subtracting before squaring, giving 197 Ω.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is at resonance when
options: X_L = X_C, so the impedance falls to R and the current is a maximum.
X_L = R, so the phase angle is 45° and the power factor is 0.707.
X_C is a maximum, so the impedance is greatest and the current least.
R = 0, so the circuit dissipates no real power at all.
questions.why: Why A is right: at resonance X_L = X_C, the reactances cancel, Z falls to its minimum value R, the current reaches its maximum V/R, φ = 0 and the power factor is 1. Why the others are wrong: B sets X_L = R, which gives a 45° phase angle but is not resonance · C reverses the whole picture; at resonance the impedance is least and the current greatest · D confuses zero resistance with zero net reactance.

questions.q: A series circuit has L = 0.100 H and C = 20.0 μF. Its resonant frequency is
options: 707 Hz
113 Hz
questions.why: Why C is right: LC = (0.100)(20.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶, √(LC) = 1.414 × 10⁻³, so f₀ = 1/(2π × 1.414 × 10⁻³) = 113 Hz. Why the others are wrong: A omits the square root, computing 1/(2πLC) · B gives ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 707 rad/s and calls it a frequency, forgetting the 2π · D is √(LC) itself, a time, not a frequency.

questions.q: A factory load draws 386 VA of apparent power but consumes only 141 W of real power. This means that
options: 245 W is being dissipated as heat in the supply cable.
the load is faulty, since apparent power cannot exceed real power.
the supply frequency is too low for the load to operate correctly.
the power factor is 0.365, so much of the current does no useful work.
questions.why: Why D is right: PF = P/S = 141/386 = 0.365. A low power factor means the supply carries current that does no useful work, which is why the apparent power far exceeds the real power. Why the others are wrong: A treats the 245 VA difference as cable loss, but the gap is circulating reactive power, not dissipation · B has the inequality backwards; apparent power is never less than real power · C blames the frequency, which does not enter P = VI cos φ.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is driven at a frequency well below its resonant frequency. Then
options: X_C exceeds X_L, the circuit is capacitive and the current leads.
X_L exceeds X_C, the circuit is inductive and the current lags.
the impedance is at its minimum value, equal to R.
the power factor is unity, since the two reactances cancel.
questions.why: Why A is right: X_C = 1/(ωC) is large at low frequency and X_L = ωL is small, so below resonance X_C dominates, the circuit is capacitive and the current leads the voltage. Why the others are wrong: B describes the situation *above* resonance · C claims minimum impedance, which occurs only at resonance · D claims unity power factor, which again is only true at resonance.

questions.q: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the instantaneous power
options: alternates between positive and negative and averages to zero.
stays positive throughout the cycle, averaging half its maximum.
is constant, because the resistance itself does not change.
goes negative in the half-cycle when both v and i are negative.
questions.why: Why B is right: in a pure resistor v and i are in phase, so in the positive half both are positive and in the negative half both are negative — and negative times negative is positive. The power curve never dips below zero, and its mean is half its peak. Why the others are wrong: A describes a purely reactive circuit · C confuses constant resistance with constant power; p = vi varies as sin²ωt · D is the specific error the sign argument is designed to catch. ### Week 8 — Magnetic fields and magnetic dipoles

questions.q: Magnetic field lines differ from electric field lines in that magnetic field lines
options: may cross one another in the region between two magnets.
run from the south pole to the north pole outside the magnet.
always form closed loops, running S to N inside the magnet.
start on north poles and end nowhere, running off to infinity.
questions.why: Why C is right: with no magnetic monopoles there is nothing for a line to start or stop on, so every line closes on itself, running N to S outside the magnet and S to N through its interior. Why the others are wrong: A allows crossing, which would give two field directions at one point · B reverses the external direction · D has lines beginning on poles and never closing, which is the *electric* field-line picture imported wholesale.

questions.q: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle. The result is
options: one piece that is a north pole and one that is a south pole.
two pieces, each of which has lost its magnetism entirely.
two magnets whose fields point opposite to the original field.
two shorter magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
questions.why: Why D is right: cutting a magnet produces two complete shorter magnets, each with its own north and south pole. Isolated poles have never been observed. Why the others are wrong: A is the monopole answer the question exists to test · B confuses cutting with demagnetising by heat or hammering · C invents a field reversal that cutting does not cause.

questions.q: A long straight wire carries 10 A. The magnetic flux density 5.0 cm from it is
questions.why: Why B is right: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(10)/(2π × 0.050). The π cancels: (4 × 10⁻⁷)(10)/(0.100) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, about the Earth's own field. Why the others are wrong: A leaves r in centimetres, dividing by 2π × 5.0 · C uses 4π in the denominator instead of 2π, halving the result · D is a power-of-ten slip on μ₀.

questions.q: A solenoid 0.50 m long has 1000 turns and carries 3.0 A. The flux density inside it is
questions.why: Why A is right: n = N/L = 1000/0.50 = 2000 turns per metre, so B = μ₀nI = (1.257 × 10⁻⁶)(2000)(3.0) = 7.5 × 10⁻³ T. Why the others are wrong: B mis-enters μ₀ by three powers of ten · C rounds μ₀ to 1 × 10⁻⁶ instead of 1.257 × 10⁻⁶, giving 6.0 × 10⁻³ T · D uses the total turns N = 1000 in place of the turns per unit length, the standard n-versus-N error, giving 3.8 × 10⁻³ T.

questions.q: The magnetic dipole moment of a plane current loop is
options: IA, measured in A/m², directed along the current in the wire.
I/A, measured in A/m², directed along the axis of the loop.
IA, measured in T·m², directed along the current in the wire.
IA, measured in A·m², directed along the axis of the loop.
questions.why: Why D is right: μ = IA, in ampere square metres (equivalently J/T), directed along the loop's axis — through the loop — by curling the right fingers with the current. Why the others are wrong: A has the correct formula but the wrong unit and points μ along the wire rather than through the loop · B divides instead of multiplying · C gives the unit as T·m², which is the weber, the unit of flux, and again points μ along the current.

questions.q: A vertical wire carries a conventional current straight upwards. Seen from above, the magnetic field around it runs
options: radially outwards, directly away from the wire in every direction.
clockwise, by the right-hand grip rule.
anticlockwise, by the right-hand grip rule.
vertically upwards, parallel to the current itself.
questions.why: Why C is right: grip the wire with the right hand, thumb up along the conventional current; the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above. Why the others are wrong: A gives a radial field, which is the pattern for a point *charge*, not a current · B is the left-hand answer, the direction you get by using the wrong hand · D puts B along the current, but B is always perpendicular to the wire.

questions.q: A solenoid is stretched to twice its original length while its total number of turns and its current stay the same. The flux density inside
options: halves, because the turns per unit length has halved.
doubles, because the solenoid is now longer.
is unchanged, because the total number of turns is unchanged.
falls to a quarter, because B depends on the square of the length.
questions.why: Why A is right: B = μ₀nI depends on the turns per unit length. Doubling L at fixed N halves n, so B halves. Why the others are wrong: B assumes greater length means greater field, reversing the dependence · C uses total turns N instead of n, the same error as in question 62 · D invents a square law that B = μ₀nI does not contain.

questions.q: A current-carrying loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field with the plane of the loop parallel to the field. The torque on the loop is
options: zero, because the loop lies along the field.
half its maximum value, since the angle involved is 45°.
a maximum, because μ is then perpendicular to B.
zero, because there is no net force on the loop.
questions.why: Why C is right: μ points along the loop's *axis*, perpendicular to its plane. If the plane is parallel to B then μ is at 90° to B, sin θ = 1, and τ = μB is at its maximum. Why the others are wrong: A and D both give zero by reasoning from the plane instead of the normal — and D also confuses the vanishing *net force* with a vanishing torque · B invents a 45° angle that is nowhere in the geometry. ### Week 9 — The Lorentz force and electromagnetic waves

questions.q: The magnetic part of the Lorentz force on a charge q moving with speed v at angle θ to a field B has magnitude
options: qvB cos θ, acting along the direction of B.
qB sin θ, independent of the speed of the charge.
qvB tan θ, acting along the direction of motion.
qvB sin θ, acting perpendicular to both v and B.
questions.why: Why D is right: the magnetic term is F = qvB sin θ, directed perpendicular to the plane containing v and B — not along either of them. Why the others are wrong: A uses cos θ, so it would wrongly give a maximum force when v is parallel to B, and points F along B · B drops the speed, so a stationary charge would feel a force · C uses tan θ and puts the force along the motion, which would let it do work.

questions.q: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to it. The field
options: increases the proton's speed, doing work proportional to q and v.
changes the proton's direction but not its speed, doing no work.
slows the proton to rest, turning its kinetic energy into field energy.
has no effect at all, since a magnetic field acts only on wires.
questions.why: Why B is right: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to v, so it has no component along the displacement. It does no work: the direction of the velocity changes, its magnitude never does. Why the others are wrong: A is the error printed in the Week 9 slides, that the work is proportional to q and v; a magnetic field cannot speed a particle up — only an electric field can · C has it removing kinetic energy, which is the same error with the sign flipped · D denies the force altogether, though the wire case is simply many moving charges.

questions.q: An electron travels exactly along the direction of a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is
options: zero, since sin θ = 0.
a maximum, since the electron moves along the field.
qvB, directed along the field.
qvB, directed opposite to the field, because the charge is negative.
questions.why: Why A is right: F = qvB sin θ with θ = 0 gives sin θ = 0 and F = 0. This is why charged particles spiral *along* field lines rather than across them. Why the others are wrong: B treats alignment as the maximum-force case, exactly reversing the sin θ dependence · C and D both give the full qvB and simply argue about its direction, when the magnitude is zero to begin with.

questions.q: One tesla is equivalent to
options: 1 N·m/A
1 Wb/A
1 N/(A·m²)
questions.why: Why D is right: from F = BIL, B = F/(IL), so 1 T = 1 N/(A·m). Equivalently, from F = qvB, 1 T = 1 N/(C·m/s). Why the others are wrong: A is N·m/A, which inverts the length · B is Wb/A, which is the henry, the unit of inductance · C divides by an extra metre, giving N/(A·m²).

questions.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to it. Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force gives the radius of its circular path as
options: qB/(mv)
mv²/(qB)
mv/(qB)
qvB/m
questions.why: Why C is right: setting qvB = mv²/r and cancelling one v gives r = mv/(qB). Why the others are wrong: A is the reciprocal, so it would make heavy particles curve more tightly · B forgets to cancel the v, leaving v² in the numerator · D is an acceleration-like combination, not a radius, and fails dimensionally.

questions.q: In a mass spectrometer, ions of the same charge and the same speed enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles. Ions of larger mass follow
options: a straight path, since the magnetic force does no work on them.
a circle of larger radius, since r = mv/(qB).
a circle of smaller radius, since heavier ions are deflected more.
a parabola, as a projectile does in a gravitational field.
questions.why: Why B is right: r = mv/(qB), so with q, v and B fixed the radius is proportional to m. Heavier ions sweep out larger circles, which is exactly how a mass spectrometer separates them. Why the others are wrong: A confuses "does no work" with "exerts no force"; the force is real, it merely acts sideways · C reverses the mass dependence · D is projectile motion, which needs a force of constant direction, not one that keeps turning with the velocity.

questions.q: Which is a correct property of an electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum?
options: E and B oscillate in phase, at right angles to each other and to the travel direction.
E and B oscillate a quarter of a cycle out of step with one another.
E lies along the direction of travel while B is perpendicular to it.
Its speed depends on its frequency, being greatest for gamma rays.
questions.why: Why A is right: E and B are perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the direction of travel, and they oscillate in step — peaking together and vanishing together. Why the others are wrong: B introduces a 90° phase lag between E and B, which is not the case in a travelling wave in vacuum · C makes the wave longitudinal in E, but electromagnetic waves are transverse · D makes c frequency-dependent; in vacuum every band travels at exactly 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.q: An FM station broadcasts at 95.1 MHz. Its wavelength is
questions.why: Why D is right: f = 95.1 MHz = 9.51 × 10⁷ Hz, so λ = c/f = (3.00 × 10⁸)/(9.51 × 10⁷) = 3.16 m. Why the others are wrong: A is a power-of-ten collapse of the right mantissa · B multiplies c by f instead of dividing · C mis-converts the megahertz by one power of ten, using 9.51 × 10⁸ Hz.

questions.q: The energy of a photon of green light of wavelength 550 nm is
questions.why: Why B is right: λ = 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m, so f = c/λ = 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz and E = hf = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(5.45 × 10¹⁴) = 3.62 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Why the others are wrong: A uses h/λ instead of hc/λ, dropping the factor c · C is the energy expressed in electronvolts, 2.26 eV, but relabelled as joules · D leaves λ in nanometres, so f is too small by 10⁹. ### Week 10 — Electromagnetic induction, self and mutual inductance

questions.q: Faraday's law states that the emf induced in a coil of N turns is
options: −N dΦ/dt, the rate of change of flux linkage.
−NΦ, proportional to the flux threading the coil.
−dΦ/dt, independent of the number of turns on the coil.
−N dB/dt, the rate of change of the flux density.
questions.why: Why A is right: ε = −N dΦ/dt. Each of the N turns contributes its own emf and they add in series; the minus sign is Lenz's law. Why the others are wrong: B makes the emf proportional to the flux itself, so a stationary magnet would drive a current · C omits N, the most common numerical error in this topic · D uses dB/dt without the area, so the answer would not even have the units of volts.

questions.q: A bar magnet is held motionless deep inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer reads
options: a large steady current, since the flux through the coil is large.
a small steady current, proportional to the strength of the magnet.
zero, because the flux through the coil is not changing.
an alternating current, at the natural frequency of the coil.
questions.why: Why C is right: flux alone induces nothing; only a *changing* flux does. A stationary magnet gives a constant flux and therefore zero emf, which is the observation that makes Faraday's point. Why the others are wrong: A and B both make the emf follow the flux rather than its rate of change · D invents an oscillation with no driving change.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns encloses 0.010 m². The field perpendicular to its plane rises steadily from 0.20 T to 0.60 T in 0.10 s. The induced emf is
questions.why: Why D is right: ΔΦ = ΔB × A = (0.60 − 0.20)(0.010) = 4.0 × 10⁻³ Wb, so |ε| = N ΔΦ/Δt = (200)(4.0 × 10⁻³)/(0.10) = 8.0 V. Why the others are wrong: A drops the factor N entirely · B forgets to multiply by the area, computing N ΔB/Δt = 800 V · C uses the final flux 6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb instead of the *change* in flux, giving 12 V.

questions.q: A rectangular loop lies flat in a steady, uniform magnetic field. An emf is induced in it if the loop is
options: slid sideways at constant speed within the uniform field.
rotated about an axis lying in its own plane.
carried at constant speed into a region of identical field strength.
held still while the field is held constant.
questions.why: Why B is right: Φ = BA cos θ, so rotating the loop about an axis in its own plane changes θ and hence the flux. This is precisely how a generator works. Why the others are wrong: A moves the loop within a uniform field, so B, A and θ are all unchanged and the flux is constant · C likewise moves it to a place where the field is identical, so ΔΦ = 0 · D changes nothing at all.

questions.q: Self-inductance is measured in
options: webers, since it concerns magnetic flux.
teslas, since it concerns magnetic field strength.
henries, and is defined by ε = −L dI/dt.
volts per second, since it opposes a changing current.
questions.why: Why C is right: inductance is measured in henries, defined through ε = −L dI/dt, so 1 H = 1 V·s/A. Why the others are wrong: A is the unit of magnetic *flux* · B is the unit of flux *density* — the flux/flux-density confusion · D quotes a rate of change of voltage, which is not what L relates.

questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.020 H. The current in the first changes at 50 A/s. The emf induced in the second is
questions.why: Why A is right: |ε₂| = M dI₁/dt = (0.020)(50) = 1.0 V. Units check: H × A/s = (V·s/A)(A/s) = V. Why the others are wrong: B divides the rate by M instead of multiplying · C quotes M itself, forgetting the rate of change entirely · D is a power-of-ten slip on the correct value.

questions.q: The reciprocity theorem for two coupled coils states that
options: the emfs induced in the two coils are equal and opposite in sign.
the mutual inductance equals the product of the two self-inductances.
the flux linking coil 1 is always equal to the flux linking coil 2.
the mutual inductance is the same whichever coil is driven.
questions.why: Why D is right: reciprocity says M₁₂ = M₂₁; the mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the same whichever one you treat as primary. Why the others are wrong: A describes an equal-and-opposite emf, which is not what reciprocity claims · B invents M = L₁L₂, which is dimensionally wrong · C requires the two flux linkages to be equal, which is only true for perfect coupling with equal turns.

questions.q: A large spark often jumps across the switch contacts when the current to an electromagnet is broken. This is because
options: the stored magnetic flux converts directly into a stream of electrons.
dI/dt is very large at that instant, so the self-induced emf is large.
the coil's resistance rises sharply the moment the current stops.
the mutual inductance between the coil and the switch reverses sign.
questions.why: Why B is right: breaking the circuit makes dI/dt enormous, and by ε = −L dI/dt the self-induced back-emf is correspondingly enormous — large enough to ionise the air gap. Why the others are wrong: A pictures flux turning directly into electrons, which is not a mechanism · C invents a resistance change; the resistance is unchanged · D confuses self-inductance in the coil with mutual inductance to the switch. ### Week 11 — Faraday's law, Lenz's law and Gauss's law

questions.q: Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in the direction that produces a magnetic field
options: in the same direction as the applied field, reinforcing it.
perpendicular to the applied field, at right angles to the loop.
opposing the change in flux that produced the current.
opposing the applied field itself, whatever the flux is doing.
questions.why: Why C is right: the induced current opposes the *change* in flux, not the flux and not the field. That word is the whole content of the law. Why the others are wrong: A reverses it, which would create energy from nothing · B puts the induced field at right angles, where it could not oppose anything · D opposes the applied field itself, which fails whenever the flux is *decreasing* — then the induced field must point the same way as the external field.

questions.q: Lenz's law is required by the principle of conservation of
options: charge, because the induced current must return to its source.
momentum, because the magnet and the coil push on each other.
magnetic flux, since flux lines are neither created nor destroyed.
energy, because a reinforcing current would give unlimited free energy.
questions.why: Why D is right: if the induced current reinforced the change, pushing a magnet towards a coil would produce a current pulling it in harder, then harder still — unlimited energy from one push. The opposition is what forces you to do work, and that work is the electrical energy you get out. Why the others are wrong: A, B and C name real conservation laws, but none of them forbids a self-reinforcing induced current; only the energy argument does.

questions.q: The flux through a loop, directed out of the page, is decreasing. The induced current in the loop
options: flows clockwise, so as to oppose the field that remains.
is zero, because the field is not actually being reversed.
flows anticlockwise, so as to maintain the flux out of the page.
flows clockwise, since the induced field always opposes the applied field.
questions.why: Why C is right: the flux out of the page is falling, so the induced field must *replace* what is being lost — it points out of the page inside the loop, which by the right-hand grip rule needs an anticlockwise current. Why the others are wrong: A and D both give clockwise, which produces a field into the page and would speed the decrease · D also states the standard misreading, that the induced field always opposes the applied field rather than the change in it · B claims no emf, but a falling flux is a changing flux.

questions.q: A magnetic field directed into the page through a flat loop is increasing steadily. Seen from the front, the induced current flows
options: anticlockwise, producing a field out of the page inside the loop.
clockwise, producing a field into the page inside the loop.
anticlockwise, producing a field into the page inside the loop.
clockwise, producing a field out of the page inside the loop.
questions.why: Why A is right: the flux into the page is rising, so the induced field must oppose the increase by pointing out of the page inside the loop, and a field out of the page requires an anticlockwise current. Why the others are wrong: B gives the correct grip-rule pairing but opposes the wrong thing, reinforcing the increase · C pairs anticlockwise with a field into the page, which is the grip rule applied with the wrong hand · D pairs clockwise with a field out of the page, the same grip-rule reversal.

questions.q: A flat coil is turned until its plane contains the direction of a uniform magnetic field. The flux through it is then
options: a maximum, because the field lies in the plane of the coil.
zero, because the field is perpendicular to the coil's normal.
a maximum, because θ measured from the plane is zero.
half of its maximum value, since cos 45° then applies.
questions.why: Why B is right: θ in Φ = BA cos θ is measured from the *normal*. If the field lies in the plane of the coil it is at 90° to the normal, cos 90° = 0, and the flux is zero — the edge-on case. Why the others are wrong: A and C both measure θ from the plane instead of the normal, which is the single commonest error with flux · D invents 45°, an angle that appears nowhere in the situation.

questions.q: A coil of area 0.050 m² lies with its normal at 60° to a uniform field of 0.80 T. The flux through it is
questions.why: Why D is right: Φ = BA cos θ = (0.80)(0.050)(cos 60°) = (0.040)(0.500) = 0.020 Wb. Why the others are wrong: A omits cos θ altogether · B uses sin 60° = 0.866 instead of cos 60°, measuring the angle from the plane · C divides by cos θ rather than multiplying, which would make the flux exceed its own maximum.

questions.q: Gauss's law states that the net electric flux through a closed surface equals
options: the total charge enclosed divided by ε₀.
the total charge enclosed multiplied by ε₀.
the total charge enclosed divided by 4πε₀.
the sum of all charges, inside and outside, divided by ε₀.
questions.why: Why A is right: Φ_E = Q_enclosed/ε₀. Nothing else matters — not the size of the surface, not its shape, not any charge outside it. Why the others are wrong: B multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing, which also destroys the units · C divides by 4πε₀, that is, multiplies by k, mixing Gauss's law with Coulomb's constant · D counts external charge, which contributes nothing net since its lines enter one side and leave the other.

questions.q: A closed box encloses charges of +3q, −q and +2q, and a further charge of +5q lies just outside it. The net flux through the box is
options: 9q/ε₀
6q/ε₀
4q/ε₀
4qε₀
questions.why: Why C is right: add the enclosed charges with their signs: +3q − q + 2q = 4q. The external +5q contributes nothing. So Φ = 4q/ε₀. Why the others are wrong: A includes the outside charge, giving 9q/ε₀ · B adds the magnitudes and so treats −q as +q, giving 6q/ε₀ · D has the right enclosed charge but multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing.

questions.q: A point charge sits at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface whose radius is then doubled. The net flux through the surface
options: is unchanged, because it depends only on the enclosed charge.
falls to one quarter, because E falls as 1/r².
quadruples, because the surface area grows as r².
halves, because the flux is now shared over a wider surface.
questions.why: Why A is right: flux depends only on the enclosed charge. Enlarging the surface changes nothing — E falls as 1/r² while the area grows as r², and the two cancel exactly. That cancellation *is* Gauss's law. Why the others are wrong: B follows only the falling field and forgets the growing area · C follows only the growing area and forgets the falling field · D invents a sharing of a fixed flux over a wider surface, which confuses flux with flux density. ### Week 12 — Transformers

questions.q: A transformer works on the principle of
options: self-inductance in a single coil wound on an iron core.
mutual inductance between two coils linked by a changing flux.
electrostatic induction between two plates separated by an insulator.
the motor effect, the force on a current in a magnetic field.
questions.why: Why B is right: an alternating current in the primary makes an alternating flux in the core, and that changing flux induces an emf in the secondary — mutual inductance, and Faraday's law behind it. Why the others are wrong: A names self-inductance, which is one coil acting on itself, not two coils coupled · C describes a capacitor, where no flux is involved · D names the motor effect, which is the force on a current, the reverse process.

questions.q: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 4000 turns on the secondary. Fed from a 240 V supply, the secondary voltage is
questions.why: Why D is right: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ = 4000/500 = 8, so V₂ = 8 × 240 = 1920 V. More turns on the secondary means a step-up, and the answer duly rises. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the turns ratio, giving 240/8 = 30 V and stepping the voltage the wrong way · B leaves the voltage unchanged, as if the turns did not matter · C multiplies by N₂ rather than by the ratio N₂/N₁.

questions.q: In an ideal step-up transformer, the secondary current is
options: smaller than the primary current, by the factor the voltage is raised.
larger than the primary current, by the factor the voltage is raised.
equal to the primary current, since charge must be conserved.
smaller than the primary current, by the square of the turns ratio.
questions.why: Why A is right: an ideal transformer conserves power, V₁I₁ = V₂I₂, so I₂/I₁ = N₁/N₂. Voltage and current move in opposite directions: step the voltage up and the current falls by the same factor. Why the others are wrong: B makes voltage and current rise together, which would create power out of nothing · C keeps the current equal, confusing conservation of charge with conservation of power · D squares the ratio, which is the rule for transformed *resistance*, not current.

questions.q: The core of a transformer is built from thin insulated sheets rather than one solid block in order to
options: make the core mechanically stronger and quieten the audible hum.
reduce eddy currents induced in the core itself.
raise the permeability of the iron and so strengthen the flux.
cut the I²R heating in the primary and secondary windings.
questions.why: Why B is right: a solid core would host large circulating eddy currents induced by the changing flux, wasting energy as heat. Thin insulated laminations confine those currents to each sheet. Why the others are wrong: A is the "it makes it stronger" answer, which confuses a mechanical reason with an electromagnetic one · C is false; lamination does not raise permeability, the choice of iron does · D describes copper loss in the windings, which lamination of the core does not touch.

questions.q: A transformer connected to a steady DC supply gives no output voltage because
options: direct current cannot pass through the iron core of the transformer.
the primary coil's resistance is far too low for direct current.
the flux in the core is steady, so no emf is induced in the secondary.
the two coils are not electrically connected to one another.
questions.why: Why C is right: induction requires a *changing* flux. A steady DC current gives a steady flux, dΦ/dt = 0, and no emf in the secondary — apart from a single pulse at switch-on. Why the others are wrong: A pictures current flowing through the core, but the coils are never electrically connected to it in the way this implies · B blames the primary resistance, which is a heating problem, not the reason for zero output · D is a true statement about transformers that does not explain the failure, since isolation applies equally on AC, where the transformer works perfectly.

questions.q: Electrical power is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage because
options: a high voltage pushes the power along the cable more quickly.
the resistance of a cable falls as the voltage across it is raised.
high-voltage cables can be made thinner and therefore cost less.
for a fixed power a higher voltage means a smaller current, and loss is I²R.
questions.why: Why D is right: for a fixed transmitted power P = VI, raising V lowers I, and the cable loss is I²R — proportional to the *square* of the current. Halving the current quarters the loss. Why the others are wrong: A imagines voltage as a speed of delivery · B claims resistance depends on the applied voltage, which for an ohmic cable it does not · C reverses the engineering; high voltage allows thinner cables *because* the current is smaller, but the saving that matters is in I²R loss, not in cable cost.

questions.q: A hair dryer rated 1600 W at 120 V is run from a 240 V supply through an ideal transformer. The current drawn from the 240 V outlet is
questions.why: Why B is right: the transformer is ideal, so it passes the full 1600 W. On the 240 V side, I₁ = P/V₁ = 1600/240 = 6.67 A. Cross-check: on the dryer side I₂ = 1600/120 = 13.3 A, and the ratio is 2, as a step-down transformer requires. Why the others are wrong: A is the secondary current, the current in the dryer itself, not the current drawn from the outlet · C halves the correct answer, applying the turns ratio a second time · D applies the turns ratio in the wrong direction to the secondary current, doubling 13.3 A instead of halving it.

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps 330 kV down to 11 kV on a 50 Hz line. The secondary output has a frequency of
options: 1.67 Hz, reduced in the same ratio as the voltage.
1500 Hz, raised in the same ratio as the current.
50 Hz, since a transformer changes voltage but not frequency.
100 Hz, because the flux reverses twice in every cycle.
questions.why: Why C is right: a transformer changes voltage by mutual inductance. Every voltage and current in it alternates at the frequency of the source, so the output stays at 50 Hz. Why the others are wrong: A scales the frequency with the voltage ratio, confusing what a transformer changes with what it leaves alone · B scales it with the current ratio, the same confusion inverted · D doubles it on the grounds that the flux reverses twice per cycle, which is true of the flux but not of the induced emf's frequency. --- *End of key.*
